reviews.text: The only other mystery dungeon game I've played has been the bonus mode of Ergheiz, and let me tell you... This was a blast. At first the veneer of resident evil mystery dungeon was what pulled me in, but as I played the game quickly moved, and grew past needing that to keep me engaged. (to purple hair? why if you insist!) You go into the dungeon, and can find spells, and pouches to increase your progress run by run, and coins to buy items, or reroll the stats on what you find. Each time you go back in you start at level one, but keep the spells, equipment you made it out with, and inventory upgrades. As far as story goes it's pretty light, mostly just the framework to give you a reason to explore with a few bits here, and there, or via one of the rare other npcs in this game to fill in a few mysteries, and leave you with a few questions you still want to know the answer to. There's a good mix of enemies, and while some of them are the same type (zombies in the first area in the garden area are moss zombies that can poison you for example) just when you're about to get tired of them a new set is introduced from dogs to tricky trapsters to mad scientist and their experiments, or even ghastly ghosts of the dead you never quite know what you're going to get, or face next, or what they can do. Bosses are pretty decent all told, and there's lots of fun cheeky reference to find. If you're expecting dark souls bosses I mean you know, don't, but I think for most people they'll be pretty decent, and cause a few resets until you learn the best way to deal with them. There's reasons to grind and upgrade your gear, spellbooks, and the like for as long as you want. A speedrun to 101% completion (and yes the game has more content than just 100%) took about 9 hours even knowing what I needed to do. I expect a player new to mystery dungeons can expect 15-30 depending on what they consider the end of their game. If you try to just spam space then you'll get replaced. Traps, good, and bad litter the floor and need to be worked around (or used cleverly to injure enemies). There's a lot of unique item modifiers such as letting you steal items from enemies, poison them, level them up (better loot but more powerful) and so on. There's a normal dungeon, and several post game dungeons, and secrets that unlock yet more secrets, and yet more secrets beyond that. As far as Voice acting goes they speak in the same style as simlish so you know A+ on that. Sounds are pretty basic, and fulfill the role you expect without any real negatives. Music is decent, there's a few tracks, including the secret areas that have their own music. The bonus dungeons I won't spoil save to say that they're both a step up from base game with various floors that test your mastery of the game and each floor comes with unique gimmicks like one hit kills you or the enemy, the minimap is disabled, all enemies become traps on death, and so on. And that's just one of the dungeons. Of course the graphics are very charming in that retro pixel style, and I have no real complaints as it seems to be exactly what the dev is going for. The real draw is of course the love story of the main character, and purple hair that exists entirely in my mind. She's the only other npc that bothers to leave the safety of the main room, and will tell you exactly how little she thinks of you, and helps guide you late, and post game to more secrets. Clearly it's true love, and I won't rest until our characters are at the altar. All that to say I was unexpectedly sucked into the game, and despite having no real desire to play them before I'm now thinking I might just start...at least if this dev makes any more. For the asking price I really don't think you can go wrong with HoN if any aspect appeals to you.

Been playing for 6 hours straight since release. Played the demo for 3 or 4 hours months ago, and fell in love with it. If you ever wanted to play as Jill Valentine killing zombies in Azure Dreams, this is your game! Love the 90s nostalgia (the sound effects from RE menus to Final Fantasy spell casting). The progression is interesting: you lose your levels every restart in classic roguelike fashion, but keep your weapons and items if you retreat and can keep them in an item box, as well as sell and reroll them eventually. I would like to see more customization and progress with the weapons. I wish I felt more attached to them. Maybe something like custom weapon/bullet mods like Parasite Eve? Still, worth way more than the 11 bucks I paid for it. If you ever wanted to play as Jill Valentine killing zombies in Azure Dreams, this is your game!

Hot off the presses just in time for Halloween season, House of Necrosis is an exceptional indie game and one of my most anticipated games from the last Next Fest. This game is so well made, I'm honestly baffled as to how it came out without more fanfare. Its ability to run on any hardware and its relatively low cost of $15.49 CAD (or your regional equivalent) are also great selling points, to be sure As a game first and foremost, the experience is great. For all intents and purposes, it's just a Mystery Dungeon game. For people unfamiliar with those games, its a top down, grid-based roguelike where you go through ever changing dungeons while kicking the ♥♥♥♥ out of things (in this case, zombies and animals and trees???). It's turn-based, and the enemies don't do nothing until you do something. You have both a melee attack as well as a ranged firearm, the gun only being operable when there is a stack of ammunition in your backpack. And not only can you have a wide variety of melee and ranged weapons, but they can come with modifiers that enhance the play experience further (I have a sword that has a chance to heal on hit, as well as explode whenever I throw it at someone). But a lot of the fun comes from the plethora of items at your disposable. Items that you can use, abuse, ingest and throw for varying effects. A healing item to stave off the plenty harmful status effects? Check. A throwing item that pushes the enemy backwards? You got it. A dangerous, unidentified jar of liquid? Drink it or throw it, hope its what you want. You can even find these magical grimoires that allow you to learn spells permanently. Whether it be a teleport or a room-wide damage debuff for enemies or even just a heal, they're a good back-up source when your inventory runs dry. Be warned though, this game can get very difficult, either through bad RNG or overwhelming numbers, and death means the loss of everything you had on you. Play carefully. The audio-visual aspect of this game is also nigh perfect. In terms of the aesthetic, its Resident Evil 1 all over again in the best ways. Note for note, from the mansion itself to the surrounding area, it's unapologetically proud of its RE1 inspiration. Even the transitional door from room to room is the same door opening style animation from those games. Hell, the dev went out of their way to recreate the tank controls for the out-of-dungeon sections, which I have nothing but the utmost respect for. Graphically, this game tickles my brain in all the right ways. I normally have problems with games that are labelled as "PSX-inspired". Not for any faults with their creator or gameplay or whatnot, but because the models look way too nice to be from the PS1 era, and they overcorrect with crummy visual filters. I'm happy to say that this game really does just FEEL like it was a lost product of that generation. The models are so low fidelity, yet they just ooze charm and personality. Even the menus play into this old PS1 feeling, with the load game function mimicking a memory card load. It made me smile so bright seeing "Checking Memory Card, Do Not Pull Out the Memory Card" pop up on my screen. Musically, its all so creepy, and perfectly fitting the ♥♥♥♥♥♥ up situation the main character has found herself in. The sound effects are even better, with amazing feedback for every single possible action. Monster noises are perfectly crafted to emulate that cheesy PS1 horror game vibe. It all comes together to form one cohesive yet beautiful package. Yeah don't sleep on this, if you like the Mystery Dungeon games you will like this. If not, still worth a try at least <3

Demo: Played the demo. It was fun and enjoyable. I made a Gun Build with "unlimited" ammo.(Gun kills refunds ammo). Game Release: They nerfed the [Refund Ammo on Kill] to a [CHANCE to Refund Ammo on Kill] (A very low chance BTW). Making a Gun Build useless since ammunition is so rare to find and every enemy eats bullets like nothing. "So why not make a Melee Build then?" You may ask. Well I did. Melee weapons do about the same as guns so it takes several hits to kill but instead you have to be next to them (in most cases). I tried a Healing Build. Heal Hp on damage dealt to enemies, along with Gain Enrage (attack buff) when I heal. However, like with the Gun build, it's a "CHANCE" to heal when dealing damage to enemies and a "CHANCE" to gain Enrage whenever I'm healed. Both have low chances to trigger so it's not worth even using any of these on your gear. It's like you have to toss a coin and get two heads in a row just trigger the Enrage buff. A "CHANCE" for a buff that only last about 3 turns. At this point you might you might as well use this more consistent build below. The Best Build I found to be consistent is the "Glass Cannon build". Just find any armor with [Do double damage but also take double damage] while keeping Confusing Hexes on hand to throw it at enemies (even at bosses as it cancels their red area attacks) and you'll have a easy time going through the floors. Just don't get hit, though you'll survive most attacks at full Health. Enemies: Most enemies has a unique attack/gimmick to them and that's a good thing. But there are so many enemies that getaway with so much. Some enemies just straight out get buffs or even steals your items just by attacking you and not having them wait a turn or even warn the player of their actions. So how to counter-play them and their mechanics? Kill them using the Glass cannon build like I stated above. That's it. It's all about killing the monster before they even have a chance hit you. You can't interrupt them because you can't see them coming or avoid them without one-shotting them. However, there are a few enemies who do attack with red zones that warns the players but those mostly are reserved for Bosses. At least those can be telegraphed and are fun to fight. Movement: There are no diagonal movement meaning fighting in a room requires only 4 enemies to box you in and get trapped. Hopefully you don't get stuck in a corner in which it only takes 2 enemies. So the best way to avoid this is to fight at the entrance of room where only one enemy can hit you. But since every room has more than one monster, 90% of the time this is how you'll be playing for the rest of the game. Items: My personal grips There isn't any point of picking up colored serums or any locked boxes. Sure I dealt with these types of items before in other Mystery dungeon games before and I use them even without Identifying their effects. But 75% of the time they hurt me more than help me. Yes I can just carry Encyclopedia and keys with me to minimalize the chance of the bad RNG but then there's no room for looting gear and weapons. Even if I reveal the effects of the serums and have keys to safely open boxes, I can just carry stacks of (10x)herbs while picking new gear instead. Finding Item Pouches to expand the inventory are rare to find can be expensive to buy in the shop when you don't have proper gear for dungeon diving. Conclusion: (10 hours of game time and currently in the 4th Area of dungeons at the time of this review and may change this review as I play more) Fun but it's mainly do to the type of genre of game. I enjoyed atmosphere, the aesthetics, and the replayability. You can see where the Developer gets their inspiration and I love what they did with it. But the unavoidable enemies nuisances and the limited movement holds the game back. Go play the demo. If you enjoy demo then buy the game and support the Developer but know that (in my opinion) the demo was more creative in character builds than the full release. 6/10. For Reference: I played Mystery Dungeons games before playing this game such as: Pokemon Mystery Dungeons and Chocobo Mystery Dungeon games. Edited: on 10/8/25 Finished the game in 14 hrs of game of game time: After being bless with a good RNG Gear, I was able to one-shot most enemies in the final dungeon going with "Glass Cannon" build. After beating the boss and seeing the end credits it was fun and replayable. I will continue playing the game and explore the post game. But I still hope the developer updates the game so players can play how they want to and how they interact with game with their creativity. Another Note: I don't know if this feature that is intended or not but I was hoarding lots of Invisible Serums in my inventory in between runs. When I return to the hub my Invisible turns back into a Unkown colored Serum. I was like, okay i just have to identify it again so i did. But my entire stack of Invisible Serum turned into a Poison Serum. So is there any point of holding serums in your inventory. I need answers if this was intended or not because it's not enjoyable for a good item to change into a bad item.

Game is really neat and super promising, but atm inventory restriction is waaaaaaaay too brutal (coming from a Shiren the Wanderer fan) even after 5+ upgrades, enemy spawns are excessive on later floors, I would much rather deal with 1/3 of the enemies that are 4x as strong, you end up just getting locked up in a swathe of red on the map unless you've ground out a weapon that can 1 or 2 shot a lot of stuff. I think this game has the sauce but currently is overtuned in a few deeply unpleasant ways (enemy spawn rates, enemy HP scaling, expectations of leveled up gear instead of leveled up gear being upside) and a few mechanics that are VERY feelbad but without the "I found a way to outplay them and/or utilize them to my advantage" twist that makes Shiren real special. Also just, cutting weapon and armor drop rate to 1/8 and making the average quality higher would help the flow a ton, having to juggle items every 3 steps becomes VERY tiresome, and its mandatory for optimal play which is required if you aren't grinding. Also having sooooo many different hexes not stack is bruuuuuutal. a ton of the hexes feel VERY low impact and VERY situational to the point that even an x9 stack of em feels bad for one of your 15-20 item slots. Will definitely swing back to check this out again after a few patches, but atm just too slow/grindy for me personally without the same huge skill expression of Shiren

Very tentative recommendation, since there's a few things that sour my experience with the game. I enjoyed the aesthetics of the game, and the combat was enjoyable. The variety of mods that were available for weapons and armour helped keep things interesting. What bothered me was the difficulty scaling in the later levels. It felt like even when you had high-level gear and had gone through all the previous levels, you still were never fully prepared to get to the end. The lack of space after a certain point left you feeling like you were unable to truly have an arsenal you wanted. The rarity of high-level drops that had two or three mod slots felt like a real gamble, in a negative way. The randomizer for existing mods was cute, but left you feeling like you had to grind coins to play a gacha that had no real way to choose your playstyle. I also wish there was a glossary for gear and items so that I could know what their stats like range, max level, and rarities were so that I didn't feel like I had to keep an inventory in my head of what weapon could do what. I feel the game has the potential to really hit it out of the park, but I feel I've hit a wall that I can't overcome to enjoy it any longer.

You could simplify this down to being Mystery Dungeon + Resident Evil, but that'd be skipping over the aspects of this game that really make it its own thing. Doing well at this game entails identifying enemy behavior patterns and knowing exactly when and how to move. When is it really beneficial to use your emergency exit, and when can you continue safely to potentially get more goodies to bring back. How much health is enough to survive a hit, or should you use that valuable herb right now and risk taking more damage than you healed. It's a roguelike game that encourages you to slow down and think, instead of holding the Run button and zipping everywhere.

Nowadays, pretty much every AAA company is incentivized to try and appeal to as many general consumers as possible, sacrificing artistic integrity for the sake of profit. With this in mind, it's definitely refreshing to see indie devs continue attempting to carve out niches within hyper-specific audiences. House of Necrosis in particular attempts to appeal to folks who are simultaneously fans of traditional mystery dungeon style roguelikes as well as survival horror games from the late 90s, which I suppose you could argue is a fancy and pretentious way of saying it appeals to masochists. But hey, I'm one of those masochists and I think this game is GREAT! Gameplay wise, House of Necrosis is much more similar to Pokémon Mystery Dungeon and Shiren the Wanderer than it is to Resident Evil or Alone in the Dark, as the horror aspect of the game is more so used for visual aesthetics. But both these genres of games follow very similar principles of resource management and risk-assessment, so even if you're a fan of one but not the other, you're still bound to find enjoyment here. For those who are familiar with survival horror but not with mystery dungeon roguelikes: House of Necrosis is a game where everything, including movement, is turn-based. It is also NOT a game that you can simply brute-force your way through. If you don't take time to study every enemy; how they move, how they attack, how they interact with other enemies, etc., you WILL hit a brick wall. The game also punishes impatient players with traps that are spread randomly across each area. While there are several ways to reveal these traps and ensure they are never stepped on, careless movements may just trigger the infamous "MONSTER HOUSE" which could spell the end of your run if you are not adequately prepared. Every encounter has you making strategic decisions about how you move, how you use your items, which items are even worth picking up, whether or not to spend a turn to heal, whether or not to gamble on a serum that you haven't identified yet, etc. The game constantly provides enough tension to keep you engaged while also giving you the time and space to breathe and plan out future turns, should you want or need it. Progression in House of Necrosis manifests itself in a few subtle ways. Throughout the game's labyrinthine areas, you can find rescue crystals that will teleport you back to the hub world while still retaining your items, allowing you to save the gear you collect for future runs. Death means the permanent loss of every item on your person, so making optimal use of these crystals is paramount. Each enemy also has a small chance to drop an item which permanently increases your inventory size, or a grimoire which can permanently teach you a new spell. Each enemy in the game has its own unique spell and each one learned gives you a new tool to potentially get you out of a situation that would otherwise be a checkmate scenario. House of Necrosis wears its influences on its sleeve, but it wears them like a badge of honor, acting as a lovely tribute the games that came before it while still managing to feel fresh in it's execution. I'm in the early stages of the post-game and I've yet to encounter a dull moment.

Did you play through one of the Pokemon Mystery Dungeon games and come out the other side thinking "Wow, I wish these games were good instead of just making me disillusioned with reality"? For those of us who didn't make a Lucario fursona after PMD, there's good news. House of Necrosis is a pretty interesting take on the Mystery Dungeon formula, though its difficulty and roguelike elements may end up wearing down your patience instead of being fun or exciting. Gameplay is very similar to PMD. top down tile movement, hidden traps, multiple floors with increasingly difficult enemies etc. It's set apart from PMD by actually being difficult and requiring you to strategize and take risks. The most exciting parts of this game are definitely when you need to carefully maneuver around enemies while maintaining your health and ammo. It's got a pretty good grasp of both survival horror and mystery dungeon mechanics. Downsides, the inclusion of roguelike elements including randomized gear and items being lost on death means that you may suddenly find yourself losing hours of progress because of a misclick. It's an incredibly unforgiving game, death means anything you were carrying is gone without any way to recover. Which adds a level of challenge and depth for sure, but if you're like me and you got through the main game but suddenly lost all of your high level equipment during an optional post-game dungeon because of bad luck, you may just not feel up to bothering any further. I had fun, but I don't feel obligated to re-farm my equipment for hours if it'll just get lost again. So, final word: Good PMD style game with a solid challenge and some fairly punishing roguelike elements that will. at the drop of a hat, beat you down into the dirt for a single absentminded button press.

My problem with this game is the fact that it's a simple reskin of Mystery Dungeon games. The core mechanics are directly copied from them and because of it there's tons of stuff that feels really out of place (like "hexes" and "spells"). Simply borrowing concepts from actual RE-titles (like item/herb/gunpowder combine, more distinct weapons with ammo types, etc.) would have given it a more original identity. Based on looks alone, you would never expect the game being about taking a step, swinging your melee weapon in the air (because it shoots a magical bullet at max HP and disarms traps next to you) to hit an enemy you can't see yet, taking a step, swinging melee weapon again, taking another step, and so on. If you have never played Mystery Dungeon (Shiren, Chocobo, Pokemon, etc.) games then this is a simple introduction to the genre, but as a new original title it feels more like a plain ripoff.

西林6不让我回城卷爽刷了，于是我来到了生化洋馆。 === 更新 26/3/26 玩着玩着就是想随手更新一点感想。 我现在觉得，这游戏大概有望成为我觉得刷着最爽的一款不可思议迷宫。 或许大多数人都觉得在不可思议迷宫里寻求爽刷感有点倒反天罡， 但是看看不可思议迷宫这个泛IP从诞生至今的演化，不管是跨IP联动作品，还是带数字的西林和特鲁尼克。 你敢说厂商自己没想过把这系列刷子化？你敢说就没有玩家在这个系列中寻求刷感？ 所以西林6的“重回初心”说实话在我这是贬大于褒的，我真要玩硬核的，为何不去玩点系统现代的新鲜传统肉鸽，要搞这个纯纯路径依赖的系列？ 当然，这都是题外话倒黑泥。 如果你觉得我这番话说的很有问题，那么我估计这款游戏就不太适合你，接下来的话你也不用看了。 因为接下来我要说说，为什么我觉得这款类不可思议迷宫悟到了刷的精髓。 要说爽，当然先要明白什么是不爽。 不可思议迷宫系列因为对于硬核拧巴的执念，不同的泛分支虽然都在优化刷感，但是又都总要保留些令人爽刷不起来的难受设计。 因此这里与其说是我想介绍下本游改进了哪些细节，不如说是想继续倒黑泥，悉数不可思议迷宫系统路径依赖的罪孽。 首当其冲的自然是暴食之罪。 饥饿度的设计一直在传统肉鸽中就是最受争议机制。 我自然不会审判其优劣，毕竟对于存在了几十年还无法得到结论的争论，妄下断言是没有意义的。 但是看看这些年主流的现代化传统肉鸽，几乎每一个或多或少的移除了原教旨饥饿度设计，取而代之的会用一些更有操作性的刷度控制机制。 这至少说明一件事，尽管大家无法否认饥饿度有其存在意义，但一定是已经不爽其久已。 以诸如刷新限制，可控耐久机制，疲劳消耗机制等等来取代饥饿度，都是还对肉鸽的原教旨有执着有追求的表现。 而更为简单粗暴的爽刷改进，呼之欲出。 对了，我倒了这么半天黑泥就是为了说： 这游戏把饥饿度直接删了！ 虽然也取消了呼吸回血，但是这意味着你只要能解决血量续航，就能无限爽刷。 紧随其后的是贪婪之罪。 背包负重，哈，又是一个争议了几十年不见结果的机制。 和饥饿度问题一样，现代游戏对这个问题有了很多新的看法。而且不仅限于传统肉鸽类型，任何RPG游戏都必须直面这个争议。 所以我就不废话评论这个机制了。 回到本游戏的话题，诚然游戏还是不可思议迷宫路径依赖式的背包限定格数。 但实际上游戏做了一点点小改进，却让游戏体验发生了巨大的提升。 首先，最明显的一点是，道具能堆叠了！ 卧槽，这简直是TM的史诗级质变，跨世纪大发明，不可思议迷宫的道具能TM堆叠了！ 堆叠之爽，我觉得我都不需要用再多说一个字了。 然后，我希望你先回想一下不可思议迷宫里那个壶。 对，就是那个逼壶。你放个道具要先点壶，然后点放入，然后翻页找到道具，然后选中道具，如果要多选还要选好后按确定，才能把道具放进去，要拿出来还得再做一遍的壶。 我TM就纳闷了，几十年过去游戏机都换了多少代了，你做个背包里有壶就自动多几个带功能的道具格，难道很难吗？ 回到本作话题，本作当然的，删掉了壶这东西，简单粗暴的直接搞成了背包升级格数。 粗暴归粗暴，但这才是个正常人会想到最自然的处理方式啊。 虽然不是首先了，但傲慢之罪还是不得不提。 前面也说了，不可思议迷宫这系列走到今天，总少不了仅在面子上装模作样的抵制一下永久成长的设计。这是一种傲慢。 尽管有的游戏已经等级都能直接带出迷宫了，却只会把永久强化项目放在迷宫外，而让迷宫内的效果都只能呆在迷宫内。 而本作的永久成长效果，（我目前玩到的）都是在迷宫内获取的。 像是永久学会的技能，还有我前面提过的背包升级，全都是探索中获取的道具。 成长就应该是和探索挂钩的，在游戏过程中获取的。而不应该是我TM死了后获取XX点然后滚回基地学技能点天赋。 至于等级，等级当然是要清零的啊。那些连等级能带出来的不可思议迷宫属于是碧莲都不要了（迷宫强度直接被挂钩等级数值，彻底丧失了对策性和互动感）。 接着是……额……好吧，我编不下去了。 但还有一点有意思的我想提一下：这游戏删了所有斜向行动。 不管是敌还是我，不管类型，不管是移动还是攻击还是远程还是投掷，都只能横平竖直，这个游戏里就没有斜向概念。 乍看觉得这可能是个傻逼删改，但是仔细一想。 没有斜向意味着我不会在墙角卡着被能无视地形的敌人暴打。 没有斜向意味着我最多只会被4个敌人包围，而不是8个。 而且反正没有饥饿度，我TM又不赶时间，非要斜着走干嘛？ 这么一想，突然就觉得删了斜向似乎还真的是有点道理。 总之倒了半天黑泥，提起本游戏却基本只有“简单粗暴的删除了XX机制”这种程度。 但我是真的认为，本游戏里删除或者改进的部分，确实是不可思议迷宫这个泛类型的痛点。 这游戏一开始就没有作为传统肉鸽的矜持。 能够比现有的刷子不可思议迷宫刷得更爽，我觉得这才是本游戏真正的追求。

One of the best mystery dungeon games on the Playstation finally gets a port to PC. I was leery of getting it at first since several PS1 ports have had issues, but it runs perfectly fine, AND they managed to get keyboard input working, which is nothing short of a miracle. The localization seems to have gotten a second pass, with fewer clunkers like the merchant's "house of doom" line and puns like the "Bloodhound." Visually it still looks amazing AND has widescreen support, but my only gripe is that there's no CRT filter. You can sort of tell that this wasn't meant to be played on an LED screen due to how some of the visuals are, but that's VERY minor. Not sure how many of the old bugs are still there, but the dupe trick with the Murder of Crows spell didn't work when I tried it (but that also corrupted your save file on the JP version so it was probably counted as a bug). Overall, Warkus did a good job on the port. Would recommend.

House of Necrosis is a retro-inspired horror RPG developed and published by Warkus that successfully merges classic survival horror aesthetics with roguelike dungeon exploration and strategic turn-based combat. Rather than focusing on fast-paced action, the game embraces a slower, more methodical style that emphasizes tension, careful planning, and survival. Its presentation immediately evokes memories of late-1990s horror classics through intentionally low-polygon visuals, fixed camera perspectives, and an unsettling atmosphere, while introducing modern procedural systems that keep every adventure unpredictable. The result is a distinctive blend of nostalgia and replayability that feels both familiar and refreshingly original. The game's biggest strength lies in its procedurally generated mansion, where each expedition offers a different layout filled with monsters, useful items, hidden secrets, and unexpected dangers. Instead of relying on memorized routes, players must adapt to constantly changing environments and make thoughtful decisions about how far to push into the unknown. Every new floor carries the possibility of valuable rewards or devastating encounters, making exploration consistently engaging. This ever-changing structure gives the game strong replay value while maintaining a constant feeling of uncertainty that perfectly complements its horror setting. Combat adopts a turn-based system that rewards patience and tactical thinking rather than quick reflexes. Every encounter requires players to carefully manage their health, equipment, and available resources while considering the risks of each action. Character progression gradually unlocks greater combat potential through leveling and equipment upgrades, creating a satisfying sense of advancement without diminishing the importance of strategy. Even as players become stronger, poor planning can still result in defeat, preserving the game's challenging nature from beginning to end. House of Necrosis also demonstrates a clear appreciation for classic survival horror design through its audiovisual presentation. The deliberately retro graphics, combined with atmospheric lighting and eerie environmental design, create an experience where imagination plays a major role in generating fear. Instead of relying heavily on graphic realism or constant jump scares, the game builds suspense through isolation, uncertainty, and the persistent threat lurking within the mansion. The mature content, which includes stylized violence and gore, fits naturally within the retro aesthetic and enhances the oppressive tone without feeling excessive. Another notable feature is the balance between roguelike mechanics and role-playing progression. Although every run presents randomized challenges, long-term character development encourages repeated attempts while rewarding persistence. The gameplay loop of venturing deeper into dangerous territory, collecting valuable resources, upgrading equipment, and preparing for future expeditions remains consistently satisfying. Fans of Mystery Dungeon-inspired adventures will likely appreciate how seamlessly these mechanics blend with the survival horror framework, creating an experience that feels rewarding whether players are exploring cautiously or taking calculated risks. The game's old-school design philosophy may not appeal to everyone. Players accustomed to modern conveniences or action-heavy horror games may find the slower pace, deliberate movement, and strategic combat less immediately accessible. However, those who appreciate classic PlayStation-era horror titles and methodical RPG systems will likely find these design choices to be among the game's greatest strengths. The commitment to its retro identity never feels like a gimmick, instead serving as the foundation for a cohesive and immersive gameplay experience. Overall, House of Necrosis succeeds in carving out its own niche by combining procedural dungeon crawling, tactical turn-based battles, and authentic retro horror presentation into a compelling package. Warkus has created a game that respects the classics while introducing enough fresh mechanics to stand on its own. Its unpredictable exploration, rewarding progression, strategic combat, and haunting atmosphere come together to deliver an engaging experience that will particularly resonate with fans of survival horror and roguelike RPGs. While its intentionally old-school approach may present a learning curve for some players, those willing to embrace its design will discover a memorable and highly replayable adventure. Rating: 9/10

Loot and loot and more loot, able to be taken as slow or as fast as you want, going from borderline tactical to gunnin and stabbin action just by tapping or holding a key. Take the classic turn based, dungeon crawling mechanics of games like Wizardry or Legend of Grimrock (complete with magic and random loot), then dress it up like the original Resident Evil for PS1. You play a member of a special forces unit trapped in a mansion overrun with zombies and other monsters, trying to reunite with her teammates and escape. Along the way, you'll find weapons, armor, and wacky items ranging from healing herbs to Blair Witch-style stick figures that hex creatures when thrown. Pile on roguelite elements and randomized maps and this one has some staying power.

Wow! What a game. This game is in my opinion the perfect modern representation of Shiren the Wanderer and mystery dungeon-likes. It's a great roguelike if you like these games. If you haven't played any of those and like roguelikes but have only played more modern examples, this game might be kind of rough and may have a steep learning curve for you. It's basically a 1:1 copy of Mystery Dungeon games with a few exceptions. It is a little bit easier in a few ways. I've played over 1000 hours for sure of those games, so this game came very naturally to me. There is a Starcraft-like level of strategy and thinking to playing these games, even if there's only one person to control, what you're controlling is the entire screen. You just do it in the guise of controlling one person. The vibes in this game are something else. I was a teen when Resident Evil first came out. This game really nails that nostalgia. When you see that door animation, you breathe a sigh of relief because you made it. It's very addictive. All the monsters are well-designed. I'm biased because I'm accustomed to approaching all new monsters I see with a lot of caution, because I don't know what they can do yet. This genre is very unforgiving in that way. Pain is the best teacher, and in this case, in this genre, it's pretty much the only teacher. That might be very difficult for some people to swallow. This genre is about steady perserverance. I'm old now. I could emulate Shiren the Wanderer or play some incarnation of it on Steam. Right now, I'm really happy with this game. I don't need that much depth, I just really like the core gameplay loop of Mystery Dungeon games. [b]And, it runs beautifully and natively on Linux.[/b]

I'm only halfway through the game and I can easily tell this game is one of the most loyal to the genre roots as far as Fushigi no/Mystery Dungeon genre goes. Meaning, it is a lot more similar to Torneko than it is to anything like Shiren. It doesn't have Shiren's convoluted, overbloated systems. The mechanics and systems are at the perfect simple but useful and sensible level like Torneko or Pokemon Mystery Dungeon. And the horror theme is a big plus if you're into it. Access to stash after every boss fight makes this a little easier to play, to not die, to return to hub and just grind out to power creep levels. Meaning it's much more grindy than Torneko is, but also less reliant on moment to moment RNG because with enough farming you can have the items you want one way or another. This game is to Mystery Dungeon what Dredmor is to roguelikes. No needless gimmicks, no reinventing of any wheel that already works. Just a fresh look and a different theme.
